stops.name: Dartington Hall, the summer school
stops.campa: In the summer Elsa is invited to Dartington Hall in Devon, the liveliest cultural commune in Europe, to teach at the summer school where the Jooss-Leeder school, Laban's lineage in English exile, keeps the German dance alive. Poets, potters, weavers, dancers; and Reich arriving from his European rounds to join her among them. At Dartington also waits Gerd Bergersen, the young Norwegian weaver, of whom the chronicle will have more to say. The English summer folds the whole diaspora of the body into one green estate.

stops.name: Oslo, the Sexpol rebuke
stops.campa: The first crack is doctrinal. Elsa speaks her mind about the Sexpol circle: neurotics, she says, rubbish, bourgeois. Reich answers in a letter with the full weight of the founder's office: as founder of the Sexpol movement he must protest. After this she stays away from the meetings. In his journal he mourns and rages in the same week: how he loved Elsa, how her illness destroys everything, how he wants a child by her. The bions are breeding in his laboratory, and the marriage of theory and dance is straining.

stops.name: Oslo, the newspaper war begins
stops.campa: From the autumn of 1937 the Oslo press opens its campaign against Reich: month after month of mockery and denunciation, the mill of Norwegian respectability grinding the foreign doctor and his life-substance. Elsa watches the man change under it. He ceases, old friends say, to be so good a therapist; he begins to crush people; and his suspicion turns homeward. Her career, her colleagues, her separate world, all begin to look to him like the face of the outside that is attacking him.

stops.name: Oslo, the blackened eye and the hardest no
stops.campa: The jealousy breaks into the open: Reich blacks the eye of a musician colleague of Elsa's, and Elsa refuses to go home with him, taking refuge with a friend. He follows, accuses, and somehow they reconcile, but the relationship is scarred and she knows it. Soon after, he asks her whether she will emigrate to America with him. She answers no. She must get back to herself, protect her independence against his demands, and decide in freedom whether she wants him at all.
stops.quote: It was the hardest 'no' I ever had to say.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Lindenberg to Myron Sharaf, interview, Oslo 1977; Fury on Earth, p. 254

stops.name: Oslo, a place of her own
stops.campa: Reich has decided for America; in the spring Elsa separates and finds a place of her own in Oslo. There is no settlement, Reich holds that a woman able to earn has no right to alimony, and she asks for none. He writes to her in April and they meet once more, two sovereignties negotiating a border. The door is not closed: he may send for her, she may follow. But the household on Drammensveien is ended, and each keeps what each brought: he the theory, she the dance.

stops.name: Drammensveien, the last evening
stops.campa: While visa delays hold Reich in Oslo through the summer, there is a last evening together. Tonight Elsa was with me, he writes in his journal; we both knew that the separation is both necessary and tragic. There is a part of me, he writes, that she understood better than anyone else; her morals are those of a beautiful wild animal that acts in accordance with its nature. It is the truest portrait anyone ever makes of her, and it is written in farewell.

stops.name: Oslo harbor, the ship she does not board
stops.campa: The ship sails for New York with Reich aboard and Elsa on the quay of her own decision. From the sea he writes that he cried a good deal on the trip, that he misses her, that he wants her to follow. Within weeks the war closes the ocean; within months he has met Ilse Ollendorf, whose body reminds him of Elsa's. The letters go on for years: tender, chiding, then business-like, then silent. Elsa remains in Oslo with her work, her students, and the hardest no she ever said.

stops.name: Oslo, the ninth of April
stops.campa: German soldiers march down Karl Johans gate; Norway is occupied in a morning. For Elsa the trap of Berlin has crossed the sea and sprung again: a German Communist, expelled from a state opera for damaging the state, companion of the Reich's most scandalous exile, standing in an occupied capital under her own true name. She loses her theatre work. The golden age of the Oslo body is over, and the age of hiding begins.

stops.name: Oslo, underground, the marriage of convenience
stops.campa: The Gestapo begins asking after her. To blunt the investigations Elsa contracts a marriage of convenience with a Norwegian, taking a citizen's name over her endangered one: a wedding as camouflage, a ring as forged papers. She goes underground in the city she taught to move, penniless through the war winters; once she overcomes her pride and writes to Reich in America for help, and he sends twenty-five dollars. The canon records the sum without comment.

stops.name: The border forests, flight into Sweden
stops.campa: By 1944 her name stands on the lists of the wanted, an enemy of the German state hunted in an occupied land, and Elsa goes over the border the way the Resistance goes: into the frontier forests, through the snow, into Sweden. The dancer's body, trained for forty years to be exactly itself, carries her across. Behind her Oslo keeps her students, her sham marriage and her furniture; ahead lie neutral ground and the long wait.

stops.name: Sweden, hidden until the end
stops.campa: In Sweden she hides until the end of the war, one refugee among the thousands the Norwegian night has pushed over the frontier. Stateless in effect, wed in name only, twice exiled: the German who fled Germany, now the German fled out of Norway. In borrowed rooms she waits out the last winter of the Reich that expelled her from her stage eleven years before, and she outlives it, as the body outlives the doctrine that condemned it.

stops.name: Oslo, the bitter return
stops.campa: Norway is free and Elsa returns to Oslo: into a liberation with no place for her. She is German, and the freed country for a time punishes the language itself: she is persecuted as an enemy national, she who stood on the wanted lists of the Gestapo. The injustice is exact and total, and the canon does not soften it. In the summer of 1945 the woman who said no to America stands in Oslo owning nothing but the method in her body.
